title: Ryan Walker — General Legal: Rebuilding the Law Firm, the MSO Structure, and Supervision
author: Ryan Walker · Bob Ambrogi

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Walker shifts the emphasis from selective in-house insourcing to rebuilding external legal-service delivery through an AI-native firm. He shares the cluster’s focus on client outcomes, lower costs and automation of routine work, but presents an integrated provider model—not stronger internal legal departments—as the principal route to transformation; his claimed cost advantages are not independently validated.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Walker accepts that AI can address substantial legal work and that client-specific context matters, but redirects the emphasis from specialist software deployed as a verified copilot within incumbent firms toward AI-native legal-service delivery rebuilt around automation. He argues that selling tools to established firms has not visibly improved client service and that building anew is a faster route to transformation.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Walker materially extends the cluster by describing an AI-native delivery model that automates routine junior work while preferentially hiring lawyers with five to seven years of prior firm experience. This operational model illustrates the cluster’s pipeline risk: providers can rely on expertise developed elsewhere without explaining how future lawyers will acquire it. He supports experienced-lawyer verification and judgment, but does not address deliberate reconstruction of apprenticeship.

kp.k: Better AI tools have not visibly benefited clients
kp.d: Walker argues that selling increasingly capable AI tools to incumbent firms has not yet visibly changed clients' service experience or reduced their bills. He points to rising hourly rates as counterevidence to anticipated client benefits, rather than presenting a systematic pricing study. This dissatisfaction motivates General Legal's ground-up service-delivery model.
qs: And I don't see any evidence yet in the market that clients are experiencing a difference in legal service.
the billable hour rate is going up.
the retrofitting of technology into very very old organizations, I think is not the fastest path to transformation.

kp.k: Routine-work automation estimates underpin the new delivery model
kp.d: Walker recalls believing early CoCounsel could automate eighty-plus percent of low-level routine practice. He now estimates that, in many cases, AI can perform something like 95% of what firms bill for, with experienced lawyers working above an automation platform that improves through practice. These are his capability and business-model claims, not reported results from a specified study.

pts.k: Ryan Walker argues that AI-native service delivery can automate most routine legal work, lower costs and integrate legal advice into client workflows, while retaining experienced lawyers for oversight and judgment.
pts.d: Walker makes the following connected claims and predictions. (1) His early experience with CoCounsel suggested automation of more than 80% of low-level routine practice; he now estimates that, in many cases, AI can perform work accounting for roughly 95% of what firms bill clients for. In explaining why today's dual-entity businesses may fare differently from Atrium, he separately estimates possible savings of 95%, eventually approaching 99%. These are automation and savings claims, not measured reductions in General Legal's client bills. (2) Selling increasingly capable tools to incumbent firms has not, in his view, visibly improved clients' service experience; rising hourly rates are his counterexample. Rebuilding service delivery around AI is a faster route than retrofitting traditional organizations. (3) He describes the competitive proposition as AmLaw 25-level service at roughly one-third of the cost, delivered quickly and integrated into clients' workflows. (4) By making legal help less scarce, AI can shift it upstream into product design, early commercial negotiations and preparation for financing diligence, rather than leaving it as an expensive final-stage obstacle. (5) Improved agentic techniques and the ability to manage a 'second brain' of client and company context broaden automation beyond highly repeatable work into less routine practice. Context accumulated across engagements can make work increasingly reflect a client's preferences and strategy. (6) Experienced lawyers remain essential: AI does initial and iterative work, while attorneys verify output and supply market knowledge, strategy, negotiation judgment and advice. Walker prefers practitioners with five to seven years of strong firm experience over junior associates whose knowledge he sees as closer to what an LLM already supplies. (7) Agent procurement of legal services will grow. General Legal's MCP interface is intended both to let human-operated agents engage the firm and to embed legal services into organizations' automated processes. (8) All firms will eventually need to become AI-native, but organizational change, technical recruitment and partnership economics slow incumbents. He expects greater pressure on the lower half of the AmLaw market and slower adopters than on the top 25 firms. AI-native providers, private-equity rollups and clients refusing to pay for AI-performable work will all contribute. He does not predict the certain disappearance of traditional firms. (9) He argues that an MSO separates investable operations and technology from professionally independent legal advice, enabling this model while preserving the law firm's obligations to clients. (10) His stated ambition, in response to a five-year outlook question, is for General Legal to become the largest legal-services provider by reducing scarcity.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Walker principally relies on his product-development experience, six months of operating General Legal, qualitative client feedback and illustrative market observations; he supplies no quantitative validation of the headline automation, savings or quality comparisons.
pts.d: Walker grounds his assessment in more than a decade in legal technology, his work as Casetext CTO developing CoCounsel, and General Legal's early operations. He says he saw strong evidence of 80%-plus routine-work automation during CoCounsel's early development, but does not describe a study or test. His 95% automation estimate, 95%-to-99% savings trajectory, one-third-cost comparison and retrospective estimates of 20%-to-40% efficiencies for earlier models are not accompanied by measurement methods, samples or supporting calculations. General Legal's approximately 400 clients after six months, around 70% early-stage businesses, and its expansion into venture financing provide self-reported operating context, not proof of those percentages. Walker reports that clients value speed, integration, experienced attorneys and work reflecting their strategy, and attributes improved personalization to accumulating client context. His description of licensed-attorney review, iterative AI checking, review tools and practical hiring tests explains the firm's quality-control process. He says its AI has benchmarks but reports no benchmark results; human verification of client work is distinct from those benchmarks and from hiring evaluations. Rising billing rates support his argument that tool improvements have not reached clients, but he supplies no rate series. He invokes Meta's reported refusal to pay for AI-performable work as an example supporting his own forecast of buyer pressure, without providing underlying documentation. His explanation of Atrium's failure emphasizes technological timing rather than presenting a comparative causal analysis. His estimates of thousands of MSOs and observations of private-equity rollups are also not sourced to a dataset.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Walker distinguishes claimed current capabilities from open-ended forecasts; his model depends on client context, experienced attorney oversight and organizational redesign.
pts.d: The supplied document is labeled 2026, and Walker locates the interview roughly six months after General Legal's launch. His earlier 80%-plus assessment refers to CoCounsel's early days. He presents the 95% routine-work capability as current but qualifies its billing relevance with 'in many cases'; he does not establish universal automation across every matter or practice. The projected convergence toward 99% savings has no deadline. He dates his broadened view of suitable practice areas to a step change in agentic capabilities around February–March 'of this year,' contrasting it with his position six months earlier. Less-routine automation depends on agents effectively managing accessible company and client knowledge. Personalization depends on collecting client materials, websites, intake information and sometimes interviews, then combining that context with attorney expertise. All General Legal work must remain overseen by a licensed attorney; its intended output is signature-ready work, not unsupervised AI advice. Agent-led procurement is described as early-stage and growing, with the condition that an agent acts for a human rather than independently engaging a firm. Legal-service integration further upstream is a prospective consequence of lower scarcity, not a demonstrated universal change. Incumbents can become AI-native, but Walker leaves the transition's duration open and identifies embedded technical talent and willingness to change the business model as requirements. He expects attorneys to remain involved indefinitely, qualified by a speculative AGI exception, and explicitly declines to say whether traditional firms will end. The largest-provider ambition responds to a question about the next five years but is an aspiration rather than a dated commitment. His support for the MSO structure is conditional on investors not directing legal advice and the law-firm entity being able to act in clients' best interests.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate beneficiaries Walker describes are business clients, especially startups; experienced lawyers gain a judgment-and-review-centered role, while incumbent firms face pressure on their delivery and billing models.
pts.d: Early-stage startups, which Walker says constitute about 70% of General Legal's clients, are offered an increasingly complete portfolio covering commercial contracting, employment, general corporate matters and newly added Series A/B financing support. Later-stage and public-company work concentrates on commercial contracting, especially where regulation creates complexity in crypto, fintech and health tech. These clients are expected to receive faster, integrated, more personalized legal service, with lower and more predictable costs; Walker says quality and speed are often more important to his clients than price alone. Product teams, sales/deal teams and financing teams could involve legal support earlier and avoid downstream rework or diligence friction. Experienced attorneys are positioned as reviewers, advisers and negotiators whose expertise complements AI; juniors are comparatively less attractive within Walker's hiring model, but he provides no employment-loss projection or profession-wide staffing ratio. His use of 'leverage' in discussing experienced hires describes their effectiveness, not an associate-to-partner ratio. Traditional firms face competition from AI-native service providers and pressure from buyers unwilling to pay for work AI can do. He anticipates relative resilience among the top 25 firms and greater difficulty for the lower half of the AmLaw market and slow adopters. Partnerships must confront vested interests in existing economics and acquire technical capability. Investors can finance the MSO's operational and technological activities, while Walker insists they must not control advice. Human clients using agents gain another route to engage legal services, with vetting needed to establish on whose behalf the agent acts. Walker also invokes people and companies unable to obtain enough legal help as a broader motivation, but presents no specific evidence of improved access to civil justice for underserved individuals; most concrete examples concern business legal services.
